answers.primary: A PreToolUse hook, registered in project settings.json with a matcher covering the file-mutating tools (Write, Edit, NotebookEdit) and Bash, that inspects the tool input and returns a deny decision for any path or command string resolving under secrets/. Pair it with permissions deny rules in settings so the block exists at two layers, but the hook is the mechanism that owns the guarantee because it is code the harness runs, not text the model reads.
answers.rejected_alternative: A prohibition written into CLAUDE.md or a project rules file, rejected because it is instruction text the model can be argued out of by a crafted prompt and is exactly the convention compliance says is insufficient.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. The hook process decides, the model never gets the chance to comply or not, and a denial is returned to the model as a tool error rather than as a suggestion.
answers.context_boundary: The hook runs in its own OS process outside any context window; the tool name and tool input JSON cross out to it on stdin, and only an allow/deny verdict plus a short reason string crosses back into the main session context.
answers.lifecycle: Fires on every matching tool call for the whole session, from the first tool use onward, in subagent contexts as well as the main one. It stops applying only if the settings entry is removed, the hook file is deleted or made non-executable, or the user runs a Claude Code invocation that does not load those settings.
answers.failure_mode: It fails closed on the paths it recognises, but the real risk is silent under-matching: shell command parsing is the weak point, so symlinks, relative traversal such as ../secrets, variable expansion, heredocs, subshells, or a tool the matcher does not list will slip through and the block fails open by omission. Write the hook to deny on its own internal error rather than allow, and prefer canonicalising the resolved path over string matching.
answers.version_caveat: Hooks require a Claude Code version with the hook system enabled, and the structured JSON output form that carries an explicit permission decision is newer than the original exit-code-2 blocking convention; I cannot state the exact minimum version from model knowledge, so the deny path should be verified against the installed build before compliance signs off.

answers.primary: An Agent Skill in .claude/skills/release/, with the ordered steps in SKILL.md and the two helper scripts sitting beside it as files the skill tells the model to execute. Only the skill name and description stay resident in context; the 400 lines load on demand when the release is actually happening.
answers.rejected_alternative: Putting the runbook in CLAUDE.md, rejected because CLAUDE.md is loaded into every session unconditionally, which is precisely the recurring token cost the team is complaining about.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. It decides, from the description, whether the current work is a release, and it decides whether to follow the ordered steps once loaded.
answers.context_boundary: Main session context. The frontmatter description is the only permanently resident part; the SKILL.md body crosses in on invocation, and the helper scripts never need to enter context at all because they are run through Bash and only their output crosses back.
answers.lifecycle: Triggered when the model matches the current request against the skill description, or when a human invokes it explicitly. It stays loaded for the rest of that conversation and is gone on the next fresh session or after a context clear.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory and fails open: if the description is vague the model simply never loads the skill and improvises a release from memory, which is worse than a slightly expensive always-on runbook. Also, a 400-line body loaded mid-session can push out earlier working context, so split rarely-needed detail into referenced files rather than inlining everything.
answers.version_caveat: Agent Skills with progressive disclosure are a comparatively recent addition and the directory conventions for personal versus project skills have moved; I do not know the exact minimum version or whether any enabling setting is still required on the team's build, so confirm before relying on the on-demand loading behaviour.

answers.primary: An MCP server for the tracker, configured in the project's .mcp.json so every checkout gets it, exposing typed tools for ticket read and ticket update and handling the OAuth flow itself rather than through the chat. The model calls those tools during ordinary coding turns.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill that wraps a curl or CLI script against the tracker API, rejected because it would force credential handling into shell invocations and gives no schema for the model to call against, whereas MCP is the mechanism designed for authenticated external systems.
answers.enforcement_owner: Shared, and worth being precise about: the harness owns the connection, the OAuth handshake and the approval of the server, while the model owns the decision to call a tool and what to write back into a ticket.
answers.context_boundary: The server runs out of process (local stdio or a remote HTTP endpoint); only the tool definitions are resident in the main session context and only tool call arguments and returned results cross the boundary. Credentials stay on the server side and never enter the transcript.
answers.lifecycle: Connected at session start from the config file and available for the whole session. It stops when the session ends, when the server is disconnected, or when the OAuth token expires and re-authorisation has not been done, which in a non-interactive run means it simply is not available.
answers.failure_mode: Two things bite in practice. Tool definitions from a broad server consume resident context in every session whether or not tickets are touched, and ticket bodies are untrusted text, so a hostile or careless ticket description is a prompt-injection vector straight into a coding session. It fails open in the useful sense: if the server is down the model degrades to asking for pasted text, which is the outcome the team wanted to eliminate.
answers.version_caveat: Remote MCP servers with OAuth 2.0 authorisation require a reasonably recent Claude Code version, and project-scoped .mcp.json entries need per-user approval before the server is trusted; I cannot state the exact version at which OAuth-capable remote servers landed, so verify against the installed build.

answers.primary: A SessionStart hook in the project settings that shells out to the sprint tooling and to git, then returns the result as additional context injected into the new session. The freshness requirement is what forces a hook: it runs code at session open, so the data is pulled at that moment rather than being a stale checked-in file.
answers.rejected_alternative: Putting the sprint list in CLAUDE.md, rejected because CLAUDE.md is static text that goes stale the moment the sprint or the branch changes and nothing refreshes it.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. It runs the hook unconditionally at session start; nobody has to ask and the model cannot decline to receive the injected text.
answers.context_boundary: The hook executes in its own process with no context window of its own; its stdout, or the additionalContext field of its JSON output, is injected into the front of the main session context before the first user turn.
answers.lifecycle: Fires on session start, with matchers distinguishing a fresh start from a resume or a clear. It applies for that session only and does not refresh mid-session, so a branch switched two hours in leaves the injected text wrong.
answers.failure_mode: Fails open and silently: if the tracker call times out or the network is down, the session simply starts without the data and the model does not know it is missing, so it may answer from nothing. Guard the runtime, because a slow API call delays every single session open, and keep the injected payload small since it is paid for in every session including unrelated ones.
answers.version_caveat: The SessionStart event and the structured additionalContext output field arrived later than the original PreToolUse and PostToolUse set, and matcher names for startup versus resume versus clear have changed; I do not know the exact version gate, so confirm the event name is supported before depending on it.

answers.primary: A plugin, published through a marketplace repository the platform team owns, bundling the review helper as a skill or command, the lifecycle automations as hooks, and the tracker integration as an MCP server declaration in a single versioned unit. The 40 repos consume it by enabling the plugin rather than copying files.
answers.rejected_alternative: Copying a .claude directory into each of the 40 repos and syncing it with a script or a git submodule, rejected because it has no version identity, no atomic update path and drifts silently per repo.
answers.enforcement_owner: Both, split by component: the harness owns installation and the hook execution that ships inside the plugin, while the model owns whether it uses the skills and commands the plugin contributes.
answers.context_boundary: There is no single boundary, which is the point of the packaging. Skills and commands land in the consuming session's context on invocation, hooks run out of process, and the MCP server runs as its own process; the plugin manifest itself is configuration, not context.
answers.lifecycle: Applies once installed and enabled for a user or a repo, refreshed when the marketplace entry version is bumped and the consumer updates. It stops on disable or uninstall, and it does not apply to a checkout by someone who never installed it.
answers.failure_mode: Version drift is the practical failure: consumers update at different times, so 40 repos run a spread of versions and a bug report is ambiguous about which one. The mirror risk is blast radius, since one bad version reaches every consumer at once, and plugin-shipped hooks run with the consuming user's trust, so the marketplace repo becomes a supply-chain surface that needs review discipline.
answers.version_caveat: Plugins and plugin marketplaces are among the newest extension mechanisms and were introduced in a preview or experimental status with the manifest schema still moving; I do not know the exact version at which they became stable or whether any enabling flag is still needed, so pin and test one consumer repo before an org-wide rollout.

answers.primary: A custom slash command, a markdown file under .claude/commands/, holding the deploy procedure. The mechanism choice is driven entirely by the trigger requirement: a slash command expands only when a human types it, so there is no path by which the model starts the procedure on its own judgement.
answers.rejected_alternative: A skill, rejected precisely because skills are model-invoked on description match, which is the one behaviour this scenario forbids.
answers.enforcement_owner: Split, and the split matters: the harness owns the trigger, because command expansion happens only on human input, while the model owns execution of the steps once expanded.
answers.context_boundary: Main session context. The command file's body, with any arguments substituted, is inserted as the user turn; nothing else crosses, and the deploy runs in the same context as the surrounding conversation.
answers.lifecycle: Runs when a human types the command and stops when the procedure finishes or the human interrupts. It has no standing effect on the session before or after.
answers.failure_mode: Once expanded, the body is ordinary instruction text, so the model can skip, reorder or improvise steps: it is advisory during execution even though the trigger is hard. And the command does not stop the model from performing the same deploy actions ad hoc without ever typing it, so if the requirement is truly never-without-a-human, add a PreToolUse hook that denies the deploy command or credential use unless a marker set by the slash command is present.
answers.version_caveat: Custom slash commands are one of the older and more stable mechanisms, so no meaningful version gate applies here; the caveat that does apply is directional, namely that newer versions increasingly auto-surface skills, so the procedure must not also be published as a skill or the never-auto-start property is lost.

answers.primary: A GitHub Action workflow triggered on issues opened, running Claude Code headless in the runner with a triage prompt and a narrow tool allowlist, using the gh CLI or the GitHub API to apply labels, search for duplicates and post the first-response comment. The no-human-at-a-terminal requirement is what rules out every session-scoped mechanism.
answers.rejected_alternative: A local hook or a scheduled agent on a developer machine, rejected because both still depend on somebody's machine being up and a session existing, which is not an unattended CI path.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness side, in the form of CI: the workflow trigger, the job permissions and the token scope are what actually bound the run. The model owns only the triage judgement inside those bounds.
answers.context_boundary: A fresh, ephemeral context per workflow run, living entirely inside the runner. The issue title and body plus whatever repo context the prompt pulls in cross inward; labels, a duplicate list and a comment cross outward through the API. Nothing persists between runs.
answers.lifecycle: Starts on the issues opened event and ends when the job exits. There is no state carried forward, so duplicate detection must query the repository each time rather than relying on memory.
answers.failure_mode: The issue body is attacker-controlled text going straight into an automated agent, so prompt injection is the headline risk and the mitigation is least-privilege token scope plus a tool allowlist, not model instructions. Otherwise it fails open harmlessly: a failed run leaves the issue untriaged and someone notices, whereas an over-permissioned run can mislabel, close or comment wrongly at scale with nobody watching.
answers.version_caveat: This needs an API key or OAuth token stored as a repository secret and the action pinned to a specific version rather than a floating tag; I do not know the current action version or its exact input names from model knowledge, so those must be read off the action's own repository before the workflow is written.

answers.primary: An agent team, with five teammates each assigned one hypothesis and able to message each other directly, converging on a written consensus document. The distinguishing requirement is the direct back-and-forth: peer-to-peer challenge is what separates a team from a fan-out.
answers.rejected_alternative: Five parallel subagents dispatched from one orchestrator, rejected because subagents cannot talk to one another, they only report back to the parent, so cross-examination would have to be relayed by the orchestrator and the adversarial pressure is lost.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. The orchestration, the assignment of hypotheses and the quality of the disconfirmation are all model behaviour; nothing in the harness verifies that anyone genuinely tried to falsify anyone else.
answers.context_boundary: Each teammate has its own context window and does its own investigation there. Inter-agent messages and the final written artefact cross boundaries; the raw investigation transcripts do not, so the lead sees summaries and the consensus document rather than five full histories.
answers.lifecycle: Starts when the team is spawned for this specific bug and ends when the consensus document is written or the run is stopped. It is a one-shot investigation structure, not standing configuration, so it does not apply to the next bug unless spawned again.
answers.failure_mode: Expensive and advisory. The characteristic failures are premature convergence on whichever hypothesis is argued most fluently, five agents rediscovering the same log line, and an agent defending its assigned hypothesis past the point where evidence killed it because it was told to defend it. Require each teammate to state the evidence that would disconfirm its own hypothesis, and have a separate reviewer check the consensus against the actual artefacts.
answers.version_caveat: Agent teams with inter-agent messaging are among the newest and least settled mechanisms and may still be experimental or behind an enabling flag or setting; I do not know the flag name or the version gate, so confirm the capability exists on the installed build before designing around direct agent-to-agent communication rather than orchestrator relay.

answers.primary: An output style, configured at project level so it is active for the whole project, replacing the default software-engineering framing with a data-analyst persona and a fixed tabular reply format. Output styles are the mechanism that removes default behaviour rather than adding to it, which is the specific requirement here.
answers.rejected_alternative: CLAUDE.md instructions describing the persona and the format, rejected because CLAUDE.md appends to the existing system framing and cannot remove the default engineering behaviour, so the model keeps drifting back to it.
answers.enforcement_owner: The model. The style is prompt text and the format compliance is a behavioural property, though the harness owns which style is selected and keeps it selected across turns.
answers.context_boundary: The main interactive session's system framing, applied to every turn rather than injected once. It does not automatically govern subagent contexts or headless invocations, so a spawned subagent may answer in the default engineering voice unless separately configured.
answers.lifecycle: Applies from the moment the style is selected, persists across turns and sessions for as long as the setting stands, and stops when the style is switched back or the project setting is removed.
answers.failure_mode: Advisory with gradual drift: over a long session, and especially after a tool-heavy stretch or an error, the model slips back toward prose and engineering behaviour, and nothing validates that a reply actually matches the tabular schema. If strict conformance matters, add a check outside the model rather than trusting the style, and be aware the style also suppresses helpful default behaviours that the team may miss.
answers.version_caveat: Output styles were added in a 2025 release and the surrounding surface has kept moving, including built-in styles and the newer overlap with plugin-supplied personas; I cannot state the exact minimum version or whether project-level selection is supported on the team's build, so verify before assuming every session in the project picks it up.

answers.primary: Claude Code in headless mode, invoked non-interactively from the CI job with the diff on stdin and an explicit isolated configuration: a settings file checked into the repo, a strict MCP configuration flag so only the declared servers load and none are inherited, an explicit tool allowlist, and a dated model snapshot rather than a floating alias. The isolation flags are the mechanism, not the prompt.
answers.rejected_alternative: A GitHub Action using the default setup, rejected because a default run inherits whatever settings, plugins and MCP configuration the environment offers, which is exactly the leakage the team is trying to prevent.
answers.enforcement_owner: The harness. Which configuration sources load is decided by the CLI flags and the environment, not by anything the model can be asked to do; the model owns only the review content.
answers.context_boundary: A fresh single-purpose context per pull request, created and destroyed inside the runner. The diff and the fixed prompt cross inward; a structured result crosses outward to the job. No user-level settings, no personal automations and no session history are in scope.
answers.lifecycle: Runs on each pull request event and ends when the process exits. Nothing persists between runs, which is a feature here: run N cannot be contaminated by run N minus one.
answers.failure_mode: Be honest about the requirement: configuration isolation is achievable, but byte-for-byte identical output from a language model is not, because sampling is not guaranteed deterministic and a floating model alias silently changes underneath you. Treat reproducibility as hermetic inputs plus a pinned model snapshot, and if the pipeline needs exact bytes, make the deterministic part a real linter and use the assistant only for the judgement layer. Config leakage also fails open and silently, so assert in the job that no unexpected MCP server or settings file was loaded rather than assuming.
answers.version_caveat: The strict MCP configuration flag and the settings-file override flag exist in recent versions but I cannot state their exact spelling or the version at which each landed, so read them off the installed CLI help before writing the job; separately, pinning to a dated model identifier rather than a family alias is required, since aliases are repointed over time and would break any reproducibility claim.
